summary: Defines a DHCP option for IPv4 that lets iSNS clients discover the iSNS server automatically. iSNS provides discovery and management for iSCSI and iFCP storage devices. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4174 defines a DHCP option that tells a storage device where its iSNS server is. iSNS is the service that maps storage names to the addresses of the storage targets, and it also carries security policies. The option gives the addresses of the primary and backup servers and four groups of flags that say which services the server offers, who is allowed to change the discovery domains, and how the session should be protected.

questions: how to find isns server automatically
how do clients find an isns server
what does the isns dhcp option contain
subtitle: A DHCP option, number 83, that tells storage devices where to find their iSNS server and how to use it.

tldr.problem: Devices using iSCSI or iFCP needed to find their iSNS server, the service that maps storage names to addresses, and the existing DHCP options could not carry that information.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines DHCP option 83, which lists the primary and backup iSNS servers together with four bit fields: which iSNS functions the server offers, who may change Discovery Domains, the administrative settings, and the IPsec settings to use.
tldr.outcome: A storage client learns where its iSNS server is and how to talk to it from a single DHCP reply. RFC 4174 was later updated by RFC 7146.

facts.label: Minimum Length field value
facts.value: 14, or 18 when the Heartbeat bit is set

today: RFC 4174 was published in September 2005 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 7146. The option it defines is the standard way for a storage device to learn the address of its iSNS server.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv4 provides a framework for passing configuration information to hosts. Its usefulness extends to hosts and devices using the iSCSI and iFCP protocols to connect to block level storage assets over a TCP/IP network.

The iSNS Protocol provides a framework for automated discovery, management and configuration of iSCSI and iFCP devices on a TCP/IP network. It provides functionality similar to that found on Fibre Channel networks, except that iSNS works within the context of an IP network. iSNS thereby provides the requisite storage intelligence to IP networks that are standard on existing Fibre Channel networks.

Existing DHCP options cannot be used to find iSNS servers, for two reasons given in the document. First, iSNS functionality is distinctly different from other protocols using DHCP options. iSNS provides a significant superset of capabilities compared with typical name resolution protocols such as DNS. It is designed to support client devices that allow themselves to be configured and managed from a central iSNS server. Second, iSNS requires a DHCP option format that provides more than the location of the iSNS server. The DHCP option has to specify the subset of iSNS services that may be actively used by the iSNS client.

The DHCP option number for iSNS is used by iSCSI and iFCP devices to discover the location and role of the iSNS server. The DHCP option number assigned for iSNS by IANA is 83. All frame formats in the document are in big-endian network byte order, and RESERVED fields SHOULD be set to zero.

The document uses these terms. An iSNS client is a process resident in an iSCSI or iFCP device that initiates transactions with the iSNS server using the iSNS Protocol. The iSNS server responds to iSNS protocol query and registration messages and initiates asynchronous notification messages, and it stores the information registered by iSNS clients. iSCSI is an encapsulation of SCSI for a new generation of storage devices interconnected with TCP/IP. iFCP is a gateway-to-gateway protocol designed to interconnect existing Fibre Channel devices using TCP/IP, mapping the Fibre Channel transport and fabric services to TCP/IP.
sections.plainLanguage: Storage devices need a way to find the service that translates storage names into addresses. DHCP can carry that, but not in an ordinary option, because the service does much more than name lookup. So a new option was needed, and it got the number 83.

sections.title: The iSNS Option for DHCP
sections.content:
The option specifies the location of the primary and backup iSNS servers and the iSNS services available to an iSNS client. It starts with the DHCP Code field, set to 83, and a Length field, which is the number of bytes that follow it.

The rest of the option is a list of parameters. The iSNS Functions field is a bit-mapped field defining the functions supported by the iSNS servers. The Discovery Domain Access field is a bit field indicating the types of iSNS clients that are allowed to modify Discovery Domains. The Administrative Flags field contains the administrative settings for the iSNS servers discovered through the DHCP query. The iSNS Server Security Bitmap contains the iSNS server security settings. Then come the address fields: a1 to a4 hold either the IP address from which the iSNS heartbeat originates or the IP address of the primary iSNS server, depending on the Heartbeat bit; b1 to b4 hold either the primary server address or a secondary server address, again depending on that bit; and each further set of four octets specifies the IP address of another secondary iSNS server.

The Code field through the a1 to a4 address field MUST be present in every response to the iSNS query, so the Length field has a minimum value of 14. If the Heartbeat bit is set, then b1 to b4 MUST also be present, and the minimum value of the Length field is 18. The inclusion of additional secondary iSNS servers in the response MUST be indicated by increasing the Length field accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries four groups of flags and then a list of server addresses. The shortest legal reply holds one server address; a second address appears when the heartbeat flag is set, and more can be appended.

sections.title: The iSNS Functions Field
sections.content:
The iSNS Functions Field defines the iSNS server's operational role, that is, how the iSNS server is to be used. The role can be as basic as providing simple discovery information, or as significant as providing IKE/IPSec security policies and certificates for the use of iSCSI and iFCP devices. It is a 16-bit field whose bits 15 to 13 carry the flags and whose remaining bits are reserved.

Bit 15, Function Fields Enabled, specifies the validity of the remaining iSNS Function fields. If it is set to one, the contents of all other iSNS Function fields are valid; if it is set to zero, the contents of all other iSNS Function fields MUST be ignored.

Bit 14, DD-Based Authorization, indicates whether devices in a common Discovery Domain are implicitly authorized to access one another. Discovery Domains control the scope of device discovery, but they do not necessarily indicate whether a domain member is authorized to access discovered devices. If this bit is set to one, devices in a common Discovery Domain are automatically allowed access to each other, if successfully authenticated. If it is set to zero, access authorization is not implied by domain membership and must be explicitly performed by each device. In either case, devices not in a common Discovery Domain are not allowed to access each other.

Bit 13, Security Policy Distribution, indicates whether the iSNS client is to download and use the security policy configuration stored in the iSNS server. If it is set to one, the policy is stored in the iSNS server and must be used by the iSNS client for its own security policy. If it is set to zero, the iSNS client must obtain its security policy configuration by other means.
sections.plainLanguage: This field says how much the server does. It can be a simple lookup service, it can hand out security policies, and it can say that being in the same domain is enough to talk to each other.

sections.title: The Discovery Domain Access Field
sections.content:
The Discovery Domain Access bit field says which kinds of client are allowed to change the Discovery Domain configuration. Its bits 15 to 10 carry the flags, with the lower bits reserved.

Bit 15, Enabled, specifies the validity of the remaining DD Access bit field. If it is set to one, the contents of the remainder are valid; if it is set to zero, the contents of the remainder of this field MUST be ignored.

Bit 14, Control Node, specifies whether the iSNS server allows Discovery Domains to be added, modified or deleted by means of Control Nodes. Bits 13 to 10 are iSCSI Target, iSCSI Initiator, iFCP Target Port and iFCP Initiator Port. These determine whether the respective registered iSNS client, determined by iSCSI Node Type or iFCP Port Role, is allowed to add, delete or modify Discovery Domains. If they are set to one, modification by the specified client type is allowed; if they are set to zero, it is not. A node may implement multiple node types.
sections.plainLanguage: Who is allowed to change the groups of devices that can see each other? The field has one bit for each kind of device, plus one for the controller.

sections.title: The Administrative Flags Field
sections.content:
The Administrative Flags field holds the administrative settings for the iSNS servers discovered through the DHCP query. Bits 15 to 12 carry the flags, with the rest reserved.

Bit 15, Enabled, specifies the validity of the remainder of the Administrative Flags field. If it is set to zero, the remaining contents MUST be ignored, indicating that iSNS administrative settings are obtained through means other than DHCP.

Bit 14, Heartbeat, indicates whether the first IP address is the multicast address to which the iSNS heartbeat message is sent. If it is set to one, a1 to a4 contains the heartbeat multicast address and b1 to b4 contains the IP address of the primary iSNS server, followed by the IP addresses of any backup servers. If it is set to zero, a1 to a4 contains the IP address of the primary iSNS server, followed by the IP addresses of any backup servers.

Bit 13, Management SCNs, indicates whether control nodes are authorized to register for receiving Management State Change Notifications. Management SCNs are a special class of State Change Notification whose scope is the entire iSNS database. If this bit is set to one, control nodes are authorized to register for receiving Management SCNs. If it is set to zero, they are not, although they may receive normal SCNs.

Bit 12, Default Discovery Domain, indicates whether a newly registered device that is not explicitly placed into a Discovery Domain and Discovery Domain Set should be automatically placed into a default DD and DDS. If it is set to one, a default DD shall contain all devices in the iSNS database that have not been explicitly placed into a DD by an iSNS client. If it is set to zero, devices not explicitly placed into a DD are not members of any DD.
sections.plainLanguage: These four flags decide where the heartbeat goes, who hears about changes to the whole database, and whether a new device lands in a default group when nobody puts it anywhere.

sections.title: The iSNS Server Security Bitmap
sections.content:
The iSNS server security Bitmap field communicates to the DHCP client the security settings that are required to communicate with the indicated iSNS server. It is a 32-bit field with bits 31 to 25 in use and the rest reserved.

Bit 31, Enabled, specifies the validity of the remainder of the field. If it is set to zero, the contents of the rest of the field are undefined and MUST be ignored. Bit 30, IKE/IPSec, is set to 1 when IKE/IPSec is enabled and 0 when it is disabled. Bit 29, Main Mode, bit 28, Aggressive Mode, bit 27, PFS, bit 26, Transport Mode and bit 25, Tunnel Mode, each say whether that option is enabled; for Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode, a value of 1 means that mode is preferred and 0 means no preference.

If IKE/IPSec is disabled, this indicates that the Internet Key Exchange protocol is not available to configure IPSec keys for iSNS sessions to this iSNS server. It does not necessarily preclude other key exchange methods, such as manual keying, from establishing an IPSec security association for the iSNS session. If IKE/IPsec is enabled, then for each of the bit pairs Main Mode and Aggressive Mode, and Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode, one of the two bits MUST be set to 1 and the other MUST be set to 0.
sections.plainLanguage: This field says how the session to the iSNS server should be protected, including whether IPsec is used at all and which IKE mode to negotiate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For protecting the iSNS option, the DHCP Authentication security option specified in RFC 3118 may present a problem due to the limited implementation and deployment of that option. The IPsec security mechanisms for iSNS itself are specified in RFC 4171 to provide confidentiality when sensitive information is distributed via iSNS. RFC 4171 also describes an authentication block that provides message integrity for multicast or broadcast iSNS messages, that is, for heartbeat and discovery messages only.

If no sensitive information is being distributed via iSNS and an entity is discovered via iSNS, authentication and authorization are handled by the IP storage protocols whose endpoints were discovered, specifically iFCP and iSCSI. It is the responsibility of the providers of these services to ensure that an inappropriately advertised or discovered service does not compromise their security.

When no DHCP security is used, there is a risk of distribution of false discovery information, for example an iSNS DHCP option identifying a false iSNS server. The primary countermeasure is authentication by the IP storage protocols discovered through iSNS. If an attacker uses DHCP and iSNS to distribute discovery information that falsely identifies an iSCSI endpoint, that endpoint will lack the credentials necessary to complete IKE authentication successfully, and will therefore be prevented from falsely sending or receiving iSCSI traffic. When the risk of false discovery information is a significant concern and IPsec is implemented for iSNS, IPsec security associations SHOULD also be used for iSNS traffic, which is more robust than relying only on the IP storage protocols.

There is also a risk of a denial-of-service attack based on repeated use of false discovery information that causes the initiation of IKE negotiation. The countermeasures are administrative configuration of each iSNS entity to limit the peers it is willing to communicate with, by IP address range or DNS domain, and maintenance of a negative authentication cache to avoid repeatedly contacting an iSNS entity that fails to authenticate. These three measures MUST be implemented for iSNS entities when this DHCP option is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Without protection on the DHCP side, someone could point a device at a fake iSNS server. The defence is that the storage protocols authenticate the far end, and an entity should refuse to talk to peers outside a configured range and remember which ones failed.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: In accordance with the policy defined in RFC 2131, IANA has assigned a value of 83 for this option. There are no other IANA-assigned values defined by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The only registration is the option number, 83.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Number of bytes that follow. At least 14, or 18 when the Heartbeat bit is set.

fields.name: iSNS Functions
fields.desc: Which iSNS functions the servers support.

fields.name: DD Access
fields.desc: Which client types may modify Discovery Domains.

fields.name: Administrative Flags
fields.desc: Heartbeat, Management SCNs and Default Discovery Domain settings.

fields.name: iSNS Server Security Bitmap
fields.desc: The IPsec and IKE settings to use with the server.

fields.name: a1 to a4
fields.desc: The heartbeat multicast address, or the primary iSNS server address.

items.label: Function Fields Enabled
items.desc: If one, the other function bits are valid. If zero, they must be ignored.

items.label: DD-Based Authorization
items.desc: If one, devices in a common Discovery Domain may access each other.

items.label: Security Policy Distribution
items.desc: If one, the client must use the security policy stored in the iSNS server.
